newsitem.title: FRANCE: French railways see less disruption in new strike.
newsitem.headline: French railways see less disruption in new strike.

text.p: France's SNCF state railways said on Monday a strike call by the Communist-led CGT trade union could reduce services by up to a half on some main and regional lines on Wednesday.

Eurostar high-speed trains through the sub-sea tunnel between Paris and London and Thalys fast train links between Paris and Brussels should be unaffected by the strike from early Wednesday morning through to 0800 GMT on Thursday, it said in a statement.
A couple of internal high-speed links, from Paris to Lille in the north and to Bordeaux in the south-west could be cut by a third but Paris region services should be unaffected, it added.
The CGT, the largest rail union, has called for strikes in a follow-up to a 36-hour stoppage last Thursday which was organised along with the CFDT and SUD-Rail unions.
All three are protesting against rail reform plans which they see as a threat to jobs and the SNCF's rail monopoly.

The CFDT is not calling out its members this time, but planning a protest on Wednesday outside the National Assembly in Paris as the lower house of parliament examines draft legislation on the rail reforms.

The bill would create a new state holding company to take over 134.2 billion francs ($24.2 billion) out of total SNCF debts of 208 billion francs and the new company would become owner of the railway infrastructure, charging the SNCF toll fees to use it.

The protesting trade unions argue that the "break-up" of the railways could open the way for competitors to move in on the busy routes, and that the rail tolls, on top of a cost-cutting drive, augur badly for jobs and working conditions.

But CFDT rail union leader Bruno Dalberto acknowledged on Friday that the campaign was a tough one to sell to the public and its members were somewhat confused about the issues, even if they objected to the government plans generally.

Trade unions other than the CGT, CFDT and SUD-Rail accept the reform on the grounds that something urgent has to be done about the SNCF's debt, much of which was run up developing France's cherished high-speed TGV train system.

Last week's strike, while a moderate success, was not on the scale of the crippling protests in 1995, when railworkers went on strike for several weeks in November and December against government plans to reduce their right to early retirement.
The government has since dropped those plans. ($ = 5.540 French Francs)
